title: The Alcoholic Who Stopped Drinking and Found Tuberculosis Instead

sections.heading: The Patient's Story
sections.content:
He is 39 years old. Two months before this admission, he developed a low-grade, intermittent fever with evening temperature spikes, which settled with medication. A dry cough lasted about 10 days around the same time, also resolving with treatment. Alongside this he noticed breathlessness that worsened when lying flat on one side, unintentional weight loss, and loss of appetite. One month before admission, right lower chest pain began — sharp, sudden, non-radiating, and worse with exertion.

He had briefly had swelling of his feet and abdomen that resolved within two days of a prior hospital admission. He has been drinking daily for 20 years, starting at 90 mL of whisky and escalating to a full bottle a day over the last six months — but he has now been alcohol-free for two months, having developed an intolerance to it.

sections.heading: What the Work-Up Showed So Far
sections.content:
- General exam: conscious, coherent, cooperative, moderately nourished; leuconychia present, mild pitting pedal edema; no icterus, cyanosis, clubbing, or lymphadenopathy
- Vitals: afebrile, pulse 85 bpm, blood pressure 100/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, capillary glucose 101 mg/dL
- Respiratory exam: reduced chest expansion on the right (more posteriorly than anteriorly), stony dullness on percussion posteriorly and below the 4th intercostal space in the mid-axillary line, with absent breath sounds and reduced vocal fremitus and resonance in the same areas — findings consistent with a right pleural effusion
- Cardiovascular and abdominal exam: unremarkable, no organomegaly
- Investigations sent: a diagnostic pleural tap, sputum CBNAAT (a rapid TB test), and pleural fluid CBNAAT, alongside routine blood work

sections.heading: How the Story Unfolded on the Ward
sections.content:
He was started on thiamine and B-complex injections, paracetamol, pregabalin for neuropathic-type pain, and a proton pump inhibitor — treatment that continued unchanged for the first three days of admission, reflecting his alcohol-use background and the need for nutritional support during his workup.

By day three, his pleural fluid and sputum CBNAAT results had come back, confirming the cause of his effusion. His treatment was expanded to include prednisolone, a vitamin B-complex formulation, and a full three-drug course of anti-tubercular therapy, and his working diagnosis was finalized as a right-sided pleural effusion secondary to tuberculosis — a diagnosis that had taken three days of workup to nail down, layered onto his recent history of heavy alcohol use and an already vulnerable nutritional state.
